(i) unsupervised methods can learn interpretable concept representations that are competitive with the ones learned by supervised methods, and (ii) the quality of the learned representations is not affected by the number of available ground truth concept labels

(a) concept representations are more accurate when they are learned in the absence of supervision; (b) the accuracy of concept representations can be improved when the ground truth concept labels are available, at the cost of interpretability; (c) concept representations learned with ground truth labels are more interpretable than unsupervised representations, but less interpretable than representations obtained with weak supervision.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

(1) the quality of learnt concepts can be assessed in both unsupervised and supervised scenarios, (2) unsupervised methods can achieve comparable performance to the supervised ones, and (3) supervision is beneficial only when there is sufficient ground truth information available.
, in the absence of supervision, the quality of concept-based representations is not guaranteed, and that, in the supervised setting, there is a clear benefit to using disentangled representations.

The main takeaway from our work is that
concept-based methods that are not supervised by human experts may be able to learn high-quality concept representations, which is a key step towards building explainable and trustworthy AI systems.
, despite their differences, the quality of concept-based representations is a shared objective for both fields, and can be measured with unified metrics.

, when the ground truth concepts are available, the best way to evaluate concept representations is to use the metrics that are designed for disentanglement, rather than the ones used in explainable AI, which may lead to sub-optimal results.
